title: Mosaic Dawn
epigraph: The world widened on a Tuesday in April.
body: NCSA Mosaic 1.0 slipped into the wild on 1993-04-22, the first browser to marry text and images in a single window.
Campus labs hummed with the new grammar of and , and the web ceased being a physicist's notebook.
doc: Recovered log shows Mosaic 1.0 compiled on SGI Indigo; Marc Andreessen noted the build passed at 03:14 UTC.
question: What tag let pictures live beside words?

title: Hypercard Ghost
epigraph: Before the browser, there was the stack.
body: HyperCard on Macintosh taught a generation that cards could link to cards, a metaphor Mosaic borrowed for the web.
The stack metaphor survived in Mosaic's hotlist, a personal map of discovered territory.
doc: Apple donated HyperCard source to the Mosaic team in March 1993; the hotlist code bears its fingerprint.
question: What Macintosh program lent its soul to the hotlist?
clue: HyperCard on Macintosh taught a generation

title: Server Whisper
epigraph: CERN's daemon answered before the world knew to ask.
body: The CERN httpd 3.0 daemon served Mosaic's first images, a 28 KB GIF of the CERN label.
Bandwidth was measured in kilobaud; every byte was a negotiation.
doc: Tim Berners-Lee's log records the first image request at 14:22 UTC on 1993-04-22 from an SGI at NCSA.
question: What format wore the crown of the first served image?
clue: a 28 KB GIF of the CERN label

title: Unix Cradle
epigraph: X windows birthed the browser; Windows followed later.
body: Mosaic launched on Unix first -- SGI IRIX, IBM AIX, SunOS, DEC Ultrix -- each port a negotiation with Motif.
The Windows port arrived months later, carried by a team that had never seen the Unix source.
doc: Spyglass licensed the Unix codebase in August 1993; the Windows port team worked from screen captures.
question: Which window system held Mosaic's first pixels?

title: FTP Fossil
epigraph: The old protocol still carried the new world.
body: Mosaic 1.0 distributed via ftp.ncsa.uiuc.edu, anonymous login, directory /Mosaic/Unix/binaries.
Mirror sites bloomed: ftp.funet.fi, src.doc.ic.ac.uk, ftp.uu.net -- each a lifeline for slow links.
doc: Transfer logs show 4,000 downloads in the first week; the SGI binary alone weighed 1.2 MB.
question: What protocol ferried Mosaic to the first users?

title: Forms Embryo
epigraph: Input arrived before the spec was written.
body: Mosaic 2.0 alpha introduced <input> and <form> in October 1993, months before RFC 1866.
The first search boxes, guestbooks, and order forms bloomed in those untamed tags.
doc: Andreessen's mail to www-talk reveals forms were coded in a weekend to demo at the MIT X Consortium meeting.
question: What weekend project became the web's first commerce engine?
clue: forms were coded in a weekend

title: Color War
epigraph: 256 colors were a battlefield; 16 million a dream.
body: Mosaic dithered images to 8-bit palettes on Sun and SGI; the Netscape palette of 216 safe colors did not yet exist.
Designers learned to count colors like scribes counting ink.
doc: A recovered style guide from NCSA warns: 'Exceed 200 colors and the colormap flashes on 8-bit displays.'
question: How many colors did the safe palette eventually standardize?
clue: the Netscape palette of 216 safe colors

title: Cookie Seed
epigraph: State was a bug before it became a feature.
body: Mosaic had no cookies; each request stood alone, Stateless as a telegraph.
Netscape 0.9 baked the first cookie in February 1994, a magic header named after fortune cookies.
doc: Lou Montulli's notebook entry: 'Persistent client state -- call it cookie, like the UNIX fortune program.'
question: What UNIX program inspired the name of the web's memory?

title: Bookmark Relic
epigraph: The hotlist was a personal atlas before it was a cloud.
body: Mosaic's hotlist.html lived in ~/.mosaic/, a flat file of <dt><a href=> entries edited by hand.
Users traded hotlist files on floppy disks, curating the web for each other.
doc: A recovered hotlist from April 1994 contains 47 links; 39 now return 404.
question: Where did Mosaic store its map of the known web?

title: Source Covenant
epigraph: Code belonged to the university until the company formed.
body: NCSA claimed ownership of Mosaic; the developers left to form Mosaic Communications, later Netscape.
The source license forbade commercial use -- a clause that birthed the browser wars.
doc: University of Illinois board minutes record the license terms: 'No fee, no commercial redistribution without written consent.'
question: What clause in the NCSA license sparked the first browser company?
